title: Scheduled executor service
label: idb
statement:
Implement the equivalent of:

public void schedule(
    Runnable command,
    long delay,
    TimeUnit unit)

The operation schedules a one-shot action that becomes enabled after the specified delay.

Implement the concept in C#.

Explain: priority queue, delayed tasks, worker thread, blocking/waiting, condition signaling, cancellation, shutdown, thread safety, spurious wakeups where relevant.

This is a concurrency/design question, not simply a syntax translation from Java.
provenance: Supplied by you from InterviewDB — the statement above is **verbatim**. Corroboration: InterviewDB + a first-hand job-scheduler design report.
clarify: `Schedule` returns a handle, despite the `void` in the signature.
A task that throws must not kill the scheduler.
Millisecond resolution, from a monotonic clock.

flaw.ctx: You asked for a bounded blocking queue.
flaw.answer: Two defects. `if` instead of `while`: a woken consumer does not re-check, so two consumers woken for one item both dequeue → exception. `Pulse` with one shared monitor: a producer can wake another producer, and the consumer that needed waking sleeps forever. **Hung or threw in 10 of 10 trials.**
flaw.fix: `while` around every Wait; `PulseAll` (or separate conditions). See BoundedBlockingQueue.

qa.a: Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

qa.q: Does async create a new thread?
qa.a: No. `async` lets a method be suspended; `await` on an incomplete task returns to the caller and schedules the rest as a continuation. No thread exists for the waiting.

The OS completes the I/O (I/O completion ports on Windows, epoll on Linux) and the continuation is queued to the thread pool or the captured context. The thread was free the whole time — that is the point.

Cooperatively. You pass a `CancellationToken` down; APIs that accept it observe it and throw `OperationCanceledException`. Nothing is aborted from outside. Blocked primitives need a registration to wake them (BoundedBlockingQueue does this).

qa.q: Can you await inside a lock?
qa.a: No — the compiler forbids it, because the continuation may run on another thread. Use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with `Release` in a `finally` (R12 is what happens without the finally).
Red-black tree: O(log n) insert, remove, lookup; in-order enumeration.

qa.q: How do you get a floor (largest ≤ x)?
qa.a: `GetViewBetween(min, x).Max` — O(log n). There is no `floorKey` like Java's TreeMap.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Implement the equivalent of:
> 
> public void schedule(
>     Runnable command,
>     long delay,
>     TimeUnit unit)
> 
> The operation schedules a one-shot action that becomes enabled after the specified delay.
> 
> Implement the concept in C#.
> 
> Explain: priority queue, delayed tasks, worker thread, blocking/waiting, condition signaling, cancellation, shutdown, thread safety, spurious wakeups where relevant.
> 
> This is a concurrency/design question, not simply a syntax translation from Java.

A one-thread scheduler. Callers hand it work and a delay; it runs each piece of work once, no earlier than its deadline, and it does so without burning CPU while it waits.

Not a value — a component. The behaviour to get right is: correct ordering by deadline, no busy-waiting, a caller-visible way to cancel, a clean shutdown, and no data race on the shared queue.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Three things the statement leaves open, and the third is the one that catches people.

**How many worker threads?** One is enough for correctness and is the right first answer, because it makes the concurrency reviewable. A pool is the follow-up.

**What does `schedule` return?** Java returns a `ScheduledFuture`, which is how you cancel. The supplied signature returns `void`, so cancellation — which the aspect list explicitly asks about — has nowhere to live. I return a handle and say why, because a `void` signature and a cancellation requirement are incompatible.

**Should `Task.Delay` count?** In C# the four-line answer is `await Task.Delay(delay); work();`. It is legitimate production code and it is almost certainly not what is being asked, given that the statement says "not simply a syntax translation" and lists spurious wakeups. Say that the library answer exists, say why you are not giving it, then build the thing.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| One worker thread. | With a pool, tasks no longer run one at a time, so a slow task stops delaying the next one — but the work must then be handed off rather than executed by the timing thread. Single worker first; say that you know the trade. |
| `Schedule` returns a handle, despite the `void` in the signature. | Otherwise cancellation is impossible, and the statement asks for cancellation. This is a contradiction in the question and worth naming rather than resolving silently. |
| A task that throws must not kill the scheduler. | Nothing in the statement says so. If exceptions should propagate to the caller, that needs a `Task`-based API, which is a different design. |
| Millisecond resolution, from a monotonic clock. | `Monitor.Wait` takes milliseconds, so sub-millisecond scheduling is not achievable this way regardless. `Environment.TickCount64`, not `DateTime.Now` — a wall-clock step would reorder deadlines. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
There are two mechanisms and the question is really about the second one.

*The easy half.* Tasks run in deadline order, so keep them in a **min-heap keyed on absolute deadline**. Absolute, not remaining, so nothing has to be decremented. `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` in .NET does this, and tie-breaking on a monotonic sequence number keeps equal deadlines in submission order — a bare heap does not promise that, and it is the kind of thing a test targets.

*The hard half.* How does the worker wait? Two wrong answers are tempting. **Spinning** burns a core. **Sleeping in fixed increments** trades latency against CPU and gets both wrong. The right answer is a **timed condition wait**: the worker takes the lock, looks at the head of the heap, and calls `Monitor.Wait(gate, msUntilDue)`. It consumes nothing while waiting, and it can be woken early.

That last property is the observation the whole design turns on. `Schedule` calls `Monitor.Pulse` after enqueueing, because **the new task may be due sooner than whatever the worker is currently waiting for**. Without the pulse, a task scheduled for 30ms behind a task scheduled for 400ms waits 400ms. It is one line, it has no visible effect in any single-threaded test, and omitting it is the most common failure on this question.

And the reason the wait sits inside a `while (true)` re-checking the head, rather than trusting what it saw before waiting: a wake can come from the timeout, from that `Pulse`, or from nothing at all — a spurious wakeup. **The loop makes all three identical**, which is why you never need to distinguish them. That is the actual answer to "spurious wakeups" in the supplied aspect list: not "handle them", but "structure the code so they need no handling".

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** One thread per task: on `Schedule`, start a thread that sleeps for the delay and then runs the work. *O(1) per schedule, and O(n) **threads**.*

**Why not good enough.** It is correct, and it is the answer to give first precisely because it is correct — then explain why it does not survive. A thread costs about a megabyte of stack committed on demand plus a scheduler entry, so ten thousand pending timers is ten thousand threads, and the OS scheduler starts to thrash long before that. `Task.Delay` is a much better version of the same idea because it uses a timer rather than a thread, and is what I would actually ship. What neither version gives you is a place to stand for the follow-ups — cancellation, ordering guarantees, shutdown semantics and introspection all want a single owned queue.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Schedule(Action work, TimeSpan delay)` from any thread |
| TRANSFORMATION | Delay becomes an **absolute** deadline: `now + delay`. A sequence number is attached for tie-breaking. |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `PriorityQueue<ScheduledTask, (long DueAt, long Seq)>` guarded by one lock; a single background worker thread |
| ALGORITHM | The worker loops: look at the head, timed-wait until it is due, pop and run it **outside the lock**. `Schedule` enqueues and pulses. |
| OUTPUT | The work runs once, no earlier than its deadline; the caller gets a cancellation handle |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `Schedule`: compute `DueAt = now + delay`, take the lock, reject if shut down, assign the next sequence number, enqueue, **`Monitor.Pulse`**, release, return a handle.
- Worker: take the lock and enter the inner loop.
- If shut down and there is nothing to drain, return — the thread ends.
- If the heap is empty, `Monitor.Wait` with no timeout and re-check.
- Peek the head. If it is cancelled, pop it and re-check.
- If its deadline has passed, pop it and break out to run it.
- Otherwise `Monitor.Wait(gate, msUntilDue)` and re-check from the top.
- Outside the lock, re-check the cancelled flag and invoke the work inside a `try`/`catch`.

- Tasks run in **deadline** order, not submission order. Submitting a 10ms task after a 1000ms one must not delay it.
- The worker must not poll. Sleeping in a loop and checking is the answer that fails this question.
- A task scheduled **sooner** than whatever the worker is currently waiting for has to preempt that wait. This is the single most-missed requirement.
- Equal deadlines should run in submission order, which a bare priority queue does not guarantee.
- `Schedule` may be called from any thread, concurrently, including from inside a running task.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| Min-heap on `(DueAt, Seq)` | O(log n) insert and O(1) peek, which is what lets the worker decide how long to sleep in constant time. The `Seq` component is what makes equal deadlines FIFO. |
| Absolute deadlines | Nothing needs decrementing when the worker wakes, and a wake for any reason recomputes the remaining time correctly from the clock. |
| One lock, not a concurrent collection | `ConcurrentQueue` would be useless here: the worker needs to *wait on a condition* (“the head is due”), and lock-free collections give you atomicity without signalling. `Monitor.Wait`/`Pulse` is the primitive that matches the requirement. |
| A single worker thread | Makes the concurrency small enough to reason about: exactly one thread touches the heap outside `Schedule`. Throughput comes later, by handing work to the thread pool. |
| `volatile bool Cancelled` with lazy removal | Removing an arbitrary element from a heap is O(n). Marking it and skipping it when it surfaces is O(1), at the cost of holding the record until its deadline. For a scheduler that is the right trade; the follow-up covers when it is not. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`Monitor.Pulse(_gate)` in `Schedule` — the load-bearing line.** The worker may be in a timed wait for a later deadline. The pulse makes it re-read the head. Without it, correctness degrades by up to the longest pending delay, silently. If one line in this class is worth narrating out loud, it is this one.

**Why the wait is inside `while (true)`.** After any wake the code starts again from "is the scheduler shut down, is the heap empty, what is the head, is it due". So a timeout, a pulse from `Schedule`, and a spurious wakeup all take the same path and none needs to be distinguished. That is the whole answer to the spurious wakeup item on the aspect list — the structure removes the case rather than handling it.

**Running the task **outside** the lock.** `ready` is captured inside the lock, and invoked after the `lock` block closes. Running inside would block every `Schedule` for the duration of the task, and a task that schedules more work would deadlock on a non-reentrant pattern. This is the second most common bug on this question and the more serious one.

**`internal sealed class ScheduledTask` — why not private.** The public `Handle` takes one in its constructor, and C# rejects a parameter type less accessible than the method (CS0051). A small, real detail: it came out of the compiler, not out of taste. The alternative is a factory method on the scheduler.

**Lazy cancellation, and the `volatile`.** Removing an element from the middle of a heap is O(n), so `Cancel` just sets a flag. The worker skips cancelled tasks when they reach the head and checks again after leaving the lock, since cancellation can land in between. `volatile` is what makes the write visible to the worker without taking the lock — `Cancel` is deliberately lock-free so it can never block behind a running task.

**The tie-break `Seq`.** Priority is the tuple `(DueAt, Seq)`. Without `Seq`, two tasks with the same deadline come out in whatever order the heap happens to hold them, which is not FIFO and is not stable between runs. Assigning `Seq` **inside** the lock is what makes it monotonic.

**`Shutdown(bool drainPending)` — two different Java methods.** `shutdown()` runs what is queued and accepts nothing new; `shutdownNow()` discards. Rather than guessing which was meant, both are here behind one flag, and `_drain` is read in the same condition the worker already evaluates. Note the consequence: draining a task scheduled an hour out means the shutdown waits an hour — worth stating as a known limitation rather than pretending it is a feature.

**`catch { }` around the invocation.** Deliberately swallowing. One task throwing must not take the worker thread with it, because that would silently stop every future task. In production this logs; an empty catch in an interview should come with the sentence "and this would log".

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Schedule` | O(log n) | O(1) | One heap insert, under the lock |
| `Cancel` | O(1) | O(1) | Sets a flag; no heap surgery, and no lock |
| worker per task | O(log n) | O(1) | One pop, plus the wait which costs nothing |
| `Shutdown` | O(1) or O(n) | O(1) | O(n) only when discarding, which clears the heap |
| space | — | O(n) | One record per pending task, including cancelled ones not yet reached |

**Cancelled tasks keep their memory until their deadline arrives**, which is the price of O(1) cancellation. If most tasks are cancelled — a timeout-per-request pattern, where the normal case is that the request finishes first — the heap fills with tombstones and this is the wrong trade. Then you want either an index from handle to heap position for O(log n) real removal, or a timing wheel where cancellation unlinks from a bucket list in O(1) with no tombstone at all. Knowing which regime you are in is the point.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Delay of zero or negative | Clamped to 0, runs immediately. Still goes through the queue, so ordering is preserved rather than jumping the line. |
| `Schedule` after `Shutdown` | Throws `InvalidOperationException`, matching `RejectedExecutionException` in Java. |
| Cancel a task already running | Returns true but has no effect — the work has already started. Documented rather than pretended away; stopping it would need cooperative cancellation via a token. |
| Cancel twice | Second call returns false. |
| A task that throws | Caught; the worker survives and the next task runs. |
| A task that schedules more work | Works, because the invocation is outside the lock. This is the case that deadlocks a naive implementation. |
| Two tasks with identical deadlines | Run in submission order, via the `Seq` tie-break. |
| Empty queue | The worker waits untimed and costs nothing until a `Pulse` arrives. |
| Delay longer than `int.MaxValue` ms | `Math.Min(waitMs, int.MaxValue)` caps the wait; the loop simply waits again. ~24 days per iteration. |
| Clock stepping backwards | Deadlines would be mis-ordered relative to new arrivals. `Environment.TickCount64` is monotonic, which is why it is the default rather than `DateTime.UtcNow`. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**One slow task delays everything behind it. Fix it.**

The worker stops executing and starts dispatching: when a task becomes due, hand it to the thread pool (`ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem`, or `Task.Run`) and go straight back to waiting. The timing thread then does O(log n) work per task and never blocks.

*Trade-off:* You gain isolation between tasks and lose ordering **of execution** — tasks become due in order but may finish in any order, and two tasks can now run concurrently, so anything they share needs its own synchronisation. That is a real semantic change and Java makes the same one: a single-threaded `ScheduledExecutorService` guarantees sequential execution and a pooled one does not. Say which guarantee you are offering.

**Support a repeating task — scheduleAtFixedRate.**

After running, re-enqueue with the next deadline. **Fixed rate** computes it from the original start (`due += period`), so the schedule does not drift. **Fixed delay** computes it from completion (`due = now + period`), so a slow task simply spaces out.

*Trade-off:* Fixed rate preserves long-run frequency and can **burst**: if one run takes three periods, three executions are immediately due and fire back to back, which for a health check is exactly wrong. Fixed delay never bursts and drifts. Java additionally guarantees a fixed-rate task never runs concurrently with itself, which is worth matching. I would default to fixed delay and offer fixed rate explicitly — the burst behaviour surprises people in production.

**There are a million pending timers. Is the heap still right?**

A **timing wheel**: an array of buckets, each a list of tasks due in that slot, with a cursor advancing one slot per tick. Insert is O(1), and cancel is O(1) by unlinking from the bucket’s list with no tombstone. Long delays use hierarchical wheels — hours, minutes, seconds — cascading down, which is what Netty and Kafka both do.

*Trade-off:* The wheel gives O(1) insert and true O(1) cancel, and costs you exact ordering within a tick plus memory proportional to the number of slots rather than the number of tasks. It wins when delays cluster in a known range and churn is high. The heap wins when delays are arbitrary and wide, because a wheel covering milliseconds to days either needs a hierarchy or a vast array. The condition, not the name, is the answer.

**Why not `Task.Delay` and four lines?**

`await Task.Delay(delay, token); work();` gets you delayed execution, cancellation via the token, and no thread per timer — it is backed by a timer queue, so it is not the thread-per-task brute force. What it does not give you is one owned queue you can inspect, ordering guarantees across tasks, drain-versus-discard shutdown semantics, or a place to change the timing structure later.

*Trade-off:* I would ship `Task.Delay` for a handful of timers and build this for a scheduler that is a component of the system — anything that needs to answer "what is pending", "shut down cleanly", or "a million of these". What I would not do is build it while pretending the library option does not exist.

**How would you test this? It is time-dependent and concurrent.**

The clock is already injected as `Func<long>`, so ordering logic can be tested against a virtual clock with no sleeping at all. What the injected clock cannot fake is `Monitor.Wait`’s timeout, which is real time — so the behavioural tests (preemption, cancellation, survival of a throwing task, 500 tasks each running exactly once) do use real delays, with generous margins so they are not flaky on a loaded machine.

*Trade-off:* A fully virtual clock would need the wait itself to be abstracted behind an interface, which is more indirection than this class earns. Splitting it — virtual clock for the decisions, real time for the waiting — gets most of the determinism for one constructor parameter. Whether the clock is injectable at all is the tell for whether someone has maintained a component like this.
